newsitem.title: FINLAND: Surveys show improving outlook for Finnish economy.
newsitem.headline: Surveys show improving outlook for Finnish economy.

text.p: Finnish industry and business leaders are now more optimistic than earlier in the year about the outlook for the national economy and for their own companies, two surveys showed on Thursday.

The growth in confidence took place after Finland pegged the markka currency to Europe's exchange rate mechanism six weeks ago in a step aimed at underlining its commitment to European economic and monetary union (EMU).

But prospects for employment were mixed because although one of the surveys appeared to offer a glimmer of hope for Finland's unemployed, the other was less upbeat. Lower unemployment is regarded as crucial to swing influential trade unions behind Finnish EMU membership.
Business magazine Forum for Ekonomi och Teknik polled in late October top executives at Finland's 500 biggest companies and found a "dramatic increase in business leaders' optimism".
Its bi-annual survey found that 66 percent of respondents saw better prospects ahead for the national economy, up from around 20 percent in May.

Only one percent expected the overall economy to turn bleaker in the coming six months. In May, some 40 percent still expected a deterioration. Two thirds of the executives also forecast that their own companies' invoicing would increase, up from 50 percent in May, the magazine said.
The findings of a quarterly industrial barometer by the Confederation of Finnish Industry and Employers (TT) painted a brightening picture for the country's three biggest export industries.
"Early this autumn, cyclical expectations have improved significantly in the forest and metal industries, and prospects have improved somewhat also in the chemical industry," TT said.

In January-July, the metal industry -- which includes base metals, engineering and electrotechnical production -- and the forest and chemical industries together accounted for 91 percent of the value of Finnish exports, according to customs board data.
Expectations for output growth and new export order intake were especially encouraging in the forest, metal and chemical industries, TT said.

Separately, the Confederation of European Paper Industries (CEPI) supported TT's view of an improving outlook for the sector. On the basis of the third quarter information, CEPI director Klaus Grewlich said on Thursday it was possible "to indicate that the worst is probably over."
Pulp prices were firming again and paper production and prices increased, he said in Brussels.

Forum for Ekonomi och Teknik said the share of executives planning to hire new employees was slightly bigger than those mulling lay-offs. In its spring survey, companies about to cut their workforce had clearly outpaced those eyeing recruitment.
"Regarding the employment situation one cannot ... expect any rapid improvement, but a ray of hope is visible," it said.
The TT barometer, on the other hand, said all industrial sectors expected to have fewer workers at the end of 1996.
In October, when both domestic surveys were made, Finnish unemployment was 17.3 percent or 425,000 people according to labour ministry statistics.
